title: Performance Enhancing Proxies Intended to Mitigate Link-Related Degradations
summary: Surveys Performance Enhancing Proxies, devices that improve TCP performance on links with troublesome characteristics, such as satellite, wireless WAN, and wireless LAN. It discusses the tradeoffs of using them.

plainLanguage.summary: A Performance Enhancing Proxy changes how traffic is handled on a network path to improve performance over a difficult link. The memo describes the techniques and the costs to reliability, diagnosis, and security.

questions: what is a performance enhancing proxy
how does snoop improve tcp over wireless
subtitle: A survey of proxies that improve protocol performance on difficult network links.

tldr.problem: TCP can perform poorly on links with long delays, high error rates, outages, or strongly asymmetric bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: Performance Enhancing Proxies (PEPs) modify or optimize traffic on a path, for example through local acknowledgments, retransmissions, compression, or split connections.
tldr.outcome: The survey makes no recommendation for or against PEPs. It warns that some methods weaken end-to-end behavior and can conflict with end-to-end IPsec.

today: RFC 3135 is an Informational survey from June 2001, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes PEP techniques and trade-offs rather than standardizing a protocol.

sections.title: What a PEP Does
sections.content:
A Performance Enhancing Proxy (PEP) improves Internet protocol performance on a path where a link or subnetwork limits native performance. The RFC is a survey and makes no recommendation for or against PEPs.

The authors say the end-to-end principle should remain the prevailing design approach. They suggest using PEPs only in specific settings where similar end-to-end improvements are unavailable, with the user aware of and in control of the choice.
sections.plainLanguage: A PEP is a device or function that changes traffic handling to improve performance over a difficult link. The authors say users should know when it is used and be able to choose end-to-end traffic instead.

sections.title: Ways PEPs Differ
sections.content:
PEPs may work at the transport layer, the application layer, or across multiple layers. They may be integrated into one device or distributed across two or more devices, often at opposite ends of a link. A PEP may behave the same way in both directions or differently in each direction.

A split-connection PEP terminates one TCP connection and creates another toward the other endpoint. Transparency describes whether end systems or applications need changes; it does not determine whether the PEP preserves end-to-end semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: PEPs differ in where they operate, how many devices they use, and whether they split a connection. A PEP can be transparent to software while still changing how a connection behaves.

sections.title: Mechanisms for Improving Performance
sections.content:
PEPs may space acknowledgments to smooth bursts, acknowledge data locally, or retransmit lost segments from a local cache. A PEP on an asymmetric link may filter and reconstruct acknowledgments. Other techniques include tunneling, header or payload compression, handling link outages, and giving interactive traffic priority.

Compression should occur before encryption when it is intended to reduce payload size, because encrypted data hides the repetition that compression uses. A split-connection PEP may keep transport state during an outage and resume forwarding when the link returns.
sections.plainLanguage: PEPs can acknowledge or retransmit data near a difficult link, reduce data size, or prioritize interactive traffic. These methods work by changing how packets are handled along part of the path.

sections.title: End-to-End Reliability and Failure Costs
sections.content:
A PEP that keeps connection state can cause a connection to fail if the PEP fails, even when another network path exists. A PEP that acknowledges data before it reaches the receiving application can also weaken end-to-end reliability.

PEPs may delay failure detection and make ping or traceroute less accurate for TCP traffic. Most require traffic in both directions to pass through them, though acknowledgment spacing needs only the acknowledgment direction. Mobile hosts may require PEP state to move during a handoff.
sections.plainLanguage: A PEP can hide failures or lose connection state if it stops working. Early acknowledgments can also report progress before data reaches the receiving application.

sections.title: Satellite and Wireless Link Examples
sections.content:
The survey describes geosynchronous satellite links with one-way propagation delays of 240 to 280 milliseconds and round-trip propagation delay of at least 480 milliseconds. It says VSAT links can have outroute-to-inroute capacity ratios of 400 to 1 or greater; the described PEPs commonly use split connections, local acknowledgments, retransmissions, and compression.

Wireless WAN links may have low bandwidth, long delays, outages, and high cost. Wireless LANs can lose packets through errors, collisions, or handoffs. The memo describes Snoop, a TCP-aware module at a base station that caches data, retransmits locally, and suppresses duplicate acknowledgments.
sections.plainLanguage: Satellite links have long delays, wireless WAN links can be slow or disconnected, and wireless LANs can lose packets. The memo describes different PEP techniques for these conditions.

sections.title: PEPs and Network-Layer Security
sections.content:
A PEP that needs to inspect TCP or application headers may not work with end-to-end IPsec because IPsec encrypts those fields. Users may need to choose between that PEP and end-to-end network-layer security, unless the PEP is trusted and acts as an endpoint for a security tunnel.

Even when a tunnel protects traffic to and from a PEP, traffic is exposed inside the PEP while it is processed. The RFC says PEPs should be protected from attack because they can provide a place to launch denial-of-service or man-in-the-middle attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: End-to-end IPsec can hide the packet details a PEP needs to inspect. If a PEP handles decrypted traffic, users must trust and protect that device.
